c1_reading.html: Capacity costs for a typical home fell to $32 a year in 2023/24, then jumped to $217 when the 2025/26 auction cleared at $269.92 per MW-day, and reached $242 as the 2026/27 to 2028/29 auctions cleared at the price cap. That is the highest level in the record, about 1.5 times 2018/19. The market monitor attributes roughly $96 to $137 a year of it to data center load.

c1_compare.html: New England is the comparison. Its capacity auctions have little data center demand behind them (0.7 GW of data centers planned or under construction, against 132 GW in PJM), and a typical home's capacity cost there fell from $289 a year in 2018/19 to $93 in 2027/28, against $242 in restructured PJM.

c1_miso.html: In MISO, the central US grid, most utilities supply their own capacity, so auction prices reach household bills directly mainly at Ameren Illinois. There the cost has swung rather than climbed: $223 a year in 2022/23, $8 the next year, $204 in 2025/26 when the summer price hit $666.50 per MW-day, and $123 for 2026/27. MISO has 47 GW of data centers planned or under construction (2.9 MW per 1,000 homes, against 5.3 in PJM).

c1_ny.html: New York has little data center load (2.5 GW planned or under construction, 0.4 MW per 1,000 homes), yet New York City's capacity price, which sets most of Con Edison's cost, reached a record $32.59 per kW-month in May 2026 and averaged $19.14 over summer 2026. Statewide, a typical New York home's capacity cost was $125 a year for 2025/26.

c3_reading.html: Baltimore Gas & Electric's customers, in a PJM state with few large data centers of its own (0.1 GW operating in Maryland vs. 14 GW in Virginia), saw real prices rise 37% between 2019 and 2026 (+14.1% versus the same months last year). Dominion's real price changed +9% over the same period (+17.0% versus the same months last year, its first full year inside the PJM capacity auction). Texas, an energy-only market with 88 GW of new generation planned (PJM: 27 GW), was at 97, and Georgia Power at 102, on a 2019 = 100 scale.

local_note.html: What doesn't explain it. Comparing each utility with others in its own regional market and month, a 40% rise in its own commercial load goes with a −0.9% change in residential price (95% CI −1.5% to −0.2%). More sales spread fixed costs. The burden comes from regional supply shortfalls and how each market passes them through.

rel_utility.html: What about reliability? Across 1,339 utilities (2013-2025), a 40% rise in a utility's own commercial load has not gone with more outages: −2.3% in everyday outage minutes per customer (95% CI −4.8% to +0.3%) and −1.8% in the number of outages, compared with utilities in the same regional grid and year. Including major storms, −4.6%.

m_capacity_result.html: Result: for a typical home in a restructured PJM state (about 10,349 kWh a year), capacity cost was $46 a year in 2024/25, $217 ($180-$253) in 2025/26, $237 ($198-$277) in 2026/27, and $242 ($201-$282) in 2028/29: about $196 a year more than 2024/25. The market monitor's findings attribute about $96-$137 a year of it to data center load. The 2028/29 level is the highest in the series, about 5 times 2024/25 and 1.5 times 2018/19.

m_capacity_ne.html: New England. ISO New England's Forward Capacity Auctions run three years ahead with the same June-to-May years. The region-wide price fell from $9.55 per kW-month for 2018/19 to $2.59 for 2026/27, then rose to $3.58 for 2027/28; the next auction, for 2028/29, is due in 2028 after a delay for market redesign. With the same method and New England's annual energy, a typical home's capacity cost fell from $289 a year to $93. All New England states but Vermont pass auction prices through default supply. No data center attribution has been published; the region has 0.7 GW of data centers planned or under construction, about 0.1 MW per 1,000 homes against 5.3 in PJM.

m_capacity_miso.html: MISO. MISO's Planning Resource Auction is held each spring for the coming June-to-May year, with separate summer, fall, winter, and spring prices since 2023/24; seasonal prices are weighted by days. Most MISO utilities are regulated and supply their own capacity, so the site applies auction prices only where default supply buys capacity in the auction: Ameren Illinois (Zone 4). Its typical home's cost ranged from $3 to $223 a year (2022/23); for 2026/27 it is $123. No data center attribution has been published.

m_capacity_ny.html: New York. NYISO buys capacity in seasonal and monthly auctions and a monthly spot auction, priced separately for New York City, Long Island, the lower Hudson Valley (the G-J Locality), and the rest of the state. The site averages the 12 monthly spot prices in each May-to-April capability year (complete years only, through 2025/26), read from NYISO's public auction viewer each week, and uses an approximate statewide requirement of 36 GW (forecast peak of about 31.5 GW plus the 18-24% installed reserve margin, less derating). All seven large New York utilities pass these costs through, including the Long Island Power Authority through its power supply charge. A typical home's cost ranged from $47 to $126 a year; Con Edison's peaked at $261 (2023/24). New York City's spot price reached $32.59 per kW-month in May 2026.

m_pjm.html: PJM vs. the rest of the US (2020 = 0): no difference from 2017 to 2021; +3.3% in 2022, +11.1% in 2023, +11.1% in 2024, +12.7% in 2025, +15.7% in 2026. The gap opened before capacity prices spiked, consistent with 2022 natural gas prices being locked into default-supply contracts, and widened as capacity costs reached bills from mid-2025.

m_case_dominion.html: First year in the PJM capacity auction (its zone cleared at $444.26 for 2025/26). The state regulator approved a base-rate increase of $11.24 a month for a typical home in 2026, about 38% of the nominal rise; fuel and other charges are not yet separated. A new rate class for customers of 25 MW or more starts January 2027.
